# How many tiles do I need?

> Calculate floor or wall tile quantities with a visible layout waste allowance and round up to full supplier cartons so you see exact tile counts and total boxes to order.

## Calculator
- [Open the calculator](https://howmanytilesdoineed.com/): US floor: a 12 × 10 ft room (120 sq ft) with 12 × 12 in tiles and 10% waste needs 132 tiles, or 14 ten-tile boxes (140 tiles). Metric: a 4 × 3 m room (12 m²) with 30 × 30 cm tiles and 10% waste needs 147 tiles, or 15 ten-tile boxes (150 tiles).

## Guide
- [How to work out how many tiles you need](https://howmanytilesdoineed.com/guide/): step-by-step measuring, common mistakes, and ordering checklist.

## Formula and method
Tiles needed = ceiling((room area / single tile area) × (1 + waste / 100)); Boxes = ceiling(tiles needed / tiles per box); Purchased tiles = boxes × tiles per box.

Convert room dimensions and tile dimensions into matching area units, divide room area by single-tile area, multiply by one plus your layout waste percentage, and round up to whole tiles. Divide by pieces per carton and round up again to full boxes.

## Limits
This is an area-plus-waste model, not a cut-by-cut layout drawing. Grout joint width, L-shaped niches, diagonal or herringbone perimeter triangles, and large-format tile breakage increase waste. Confirm exact square footage per box and match batch/caliber codes before installing.

## Tile layout waste allowances and common tile coverage

Choose a higher waste percentage whenever tiles are laid on an angle, around fixtures, or in narrow alcoves.

| Layout pattern or tile size | Recommended waste | Coverage per tile | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Straight / stacked grid | 10% | — | Lowest cut waste; keep 5–10% intact spares |
| Brick / running bond (offset) | 10%–12% | — | Half-tile edge cuts every other row |
| Diagonal (45-degree) | 15% | — | Triangular cuts along every perimeter wall |
| Herringbone / chevron | 15%–20% | — | High edge waste and precision angle cuts |
| 3 × 6 in subway tile | 12%–15% | 0.125 sq ft (8 / sq ft) | Common kitchen/shower wall format |
| 12 × 12 in (30 × 30 cm) | 10%–12% | 1.0 sq ft (0.09 m²) | Standard bathroom & utility floor |
| 12 × 24 in (30 × 60 cm) | 10%–15% | 2.0 sq ft (0.18 m²) | Verify 1/3 offset limit for large-format tiles |

## Step by step
1. Measure the length and width of the floor (or wall width and height). Break L-shaped rooms into rectangles and add their areas.
2. Check the actual nominal and work size of one tile on the carton specification—for instance, a "12 × 12 in" tile may be slightly smaller to allow grout joints.
3. Choose a waste allowance matching your layout: 10% for straight grid layouts, 12% to 15% for brick or diagonal, and 15% to 20% for herringbone or complex cuts.
4. Enter how many whole tiles come in one carton so the final order rounds up to full boxes.

## Common mistakes
- Ordering exact net floor area with zero waste. Even simple rectangular rooms lose tiles to perimeter edge cuts and accidental breakage.
- Using 10% waste on a diagonal or herringbone layout, which creates triangular cuts along every single wall.
- Using every last tile during installation and keeping no spares—matching the exact shade and caliber years later is often impossible.
- Mixing cartons with different dye-lot (tonality) or caliber codes on the same floor or wall.

## Worked examples
### Example 1
Metric: a 4 × 3 m room (12 m²) with 30 × 30 cm tiles and 10% waste needs 147 tiles, or 15 ten-tile boxes (150 tiles).

### Example 2
US floor: a 12 × 10 ft room (120 sq ft) with 12 × 12 in tiles and 10% waste needs 132 tiles, or 14 ten-tile boxes (140 tiles).
